models_evaluated: Random survival forest pancreatic cancer risk model (refit and original)

links.outcome: C-index and calibration of original versus refit model on 2020 cohort
links.effect: Without refitting C-index ranged 0.69 to 0.84; with refitting 0.79 to 0.85 (abstract: 0.79 to 0.83); calibration improved markedly.
links.quote: Refitting the RSF model using the 2018–2019 cohort led to consistent improvements in predictive performance across all modelling configurations when evaluated on the 2020 evaluation cohort ( Table 2 ).

links.outcome: Discrimination and calibration before versus after refitting model on recent local data
links.effect: Refitting improved C-index across all scenarios (e.g., non-imputed 0.69 to 0.81) and improved alignment of predicted and observed risk.
links.quote: After refitting, the C-index improved across all scenarios, ranging from 0.79 to 0.85, with the most notable gain in the non-imputed condition (from 0.69 to 0.81).

links.outcome: Effect of recalibrating/refitting on calibration under population and temporal change
links.effect: Refitting improved alignment between predicted and observed risks; residual miscalibration remained in the 95–100th percentile (GND p < 0.001 all methods).
links.quote: Refitting improved alignment between predicted and observed risks across most groups, with residual miscalibration primarily confined to the 95–100th percentile (GND p < 0.001 across all methods), as shown in Fig. 2 .

links.outcome: Model discrimination and calibration by racial/ethnic subgroup
links.effect: C-index ranged 0.78 to 0.89 across groups; calibration poorest for Black patients, with risk underestimation.
links.quote: Calibration is poorest for Black patients, but SMI was the best among all three imputation strategies ( Fig. 3 ).

links.outcome: Coverage and performance for patients with missing predictor data
links.effect: Without imputation only about one-eighth of cohort had complete data (N=40,300 of 350,677); complete cases had higher PPV, with likely selection bias.
links.quote: In the absence of imputation, only a small fraction of the evaluation cohort had complete data for all model predictors, approximately one-eighth the size of the cohort eligible for prediction when imputation was applied.

links.outcome: Subgroup-specific calibration/PPV differences by race and ethnicity
links.effect: Calibration poorest for Black patients though PPV higher; systematic risk underestimation could reduce likelihood of being flagged for evaluation.
links.quote: This pattern is not unexpected: because the model was trained on the pooled population without subgroup-specific recalibration, the higher baseline incidence among Black patients likely contributed to systematic risk underestimation, which could reduce their likelihood of being flagged for further evaluation.

links.outcome: Runtime and feasibility of deployment pipeline across imputation methods in simulated weekly batches
links.effect: Mean imputation and execution time per batch: SME 0.71 min, IFCE 19.54 min, SMI 383.77 min; data extraction 13.30 hours.
links.quote: In contrast, SMI was not only less effective in prediction but also computationally intensive, requiring an average of over 6 h per batch (383.77 min), which may limit scalability.
